text.p: Copper turned lower with a vengeance during Monday LME kerb trading with a downturn below $2,200 triggering sell-stops and fresh selling, and prices ended at the day's lows.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau Index fell 1.95 points to 241.41.

In London, copper traders said narrowing spread backwardations, a perception that there would be another small inventory increase on Tuesday, and less concern over high upside call options being declared on Wednesday sent a volatile market lower. But conditions are seen remaining volatile, and prices may easily whip higher again.

The market weakened from the outset of afternoon trading, with losses in New York in post-Thanksgiving holiday trading augmenting the trend, and with spread premiums softening stops were eventually hit on both sides of the Atlantic.
Last kerb business was at $2,187 a tonne, down $55 from Friday's kerb close, and compared with last week's six-month peak of $2,313.
Cash/threes narrowed as well, and was around $185 at the close, against $245 on Friday and the high-point last week of $285.
Aluminium finished at $1,518, down $11 from Friday, but is still looking to consolidate after last week's advances to six-month highs. Stocks are seen lower tomorrow.
Lead was boosted by news of output losses at Doe Run's Buick secondary facility, caused by furnace problems. Prices peaked abvove $690 before settling back with copper to end at $688, still up $2.
Zinc paid little heed to news that Noranda's Heath Steele mine in New Brunswick has been closed since an accident on Friday. The market sagged in late trade and closed at $1,066, down $5.
Tin was supported around the $6,100 level, which helped to restrict losses, and last business was at $6,100, down just $10.
Nickel was partially helped by short-covering, and closed at $6,840, up $20.
Alloy was slow, but held fairly steady to close at $1,358/60 a tonne.

CBOT wheat futures were lower at midsession on disappointment the U.S. did not land a wheat sale to Pakistan, traders said. Export sources said Pakistan bought 225,000 tonnes of wheat from Australia rather than the U.S. At 1114 CST, wheat was 1/2 to 3-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with December down 3-1/2 at $3.92-1/2.
CSCE world sugar futures ended near unchanged in subdued dealings Monday, as producer-linked selling capped a light round of buying by speculators and the trade, brokers said.

Short-covering on the part of commodity funds lent some strength to the market, sustaining nearby March a notch above unchanged for much of the session. But origin selling intensified near the 10.70-mark, easily blocking a test of resistance toward 10.75-10.76. Most-active March ended flat at 10.66 cents, having ranged from 10.63 to 10.71. Second-position May rose 0.01, to 10.74, as the switches remained fairly stable.

NYMEX crude sharpened its gains Monday afternoon on a gasoline-lead rally which also pulled heating oil out of negative territory, traders said. "Gasoline lead crude higher after crude went up on technical buying," said a dealer. At 1417 EST, January crude stood 0.51 cent a barrel higher at $24.26 after buy stops were triggered above $23.95 and $24.00, traders said. January gasoline was up 1.49 cents a gallon at 66.95 cents while Janaury heat was 0.72 cent higher at 72.40 cents a gallon.

New York precious metals remained lower midday, but once opening prices moved in line with overnight levels, the market died down with volume generally modest in the first post-Thanksgiving session. By midday February gold was trading in a relatively narrow range. Volume was estimated at 10,000 lots at 1100 EST. "It was a post-holiday adjustment, if anything," said John Geraghty of North American Equity Services. At 1252 EST February gold was off $2.40 at $372.60 an ounce, traded $373.90 to $371.90. Bullion was quoted at $370.70/$371.20 an ounce.
